title: Latency-SLA driven kernel binding and epochal profile registry
creator: Jonas Meyer
description:
Problem: When onboarding large transformer variants (MHA/GQA/MoE) to the runtime we often select kernels purely by peak throughput or an ad-hoc latency test. That has led to customer regressions when input distributions shift (longer sequences, bursty single-request latency) and to frequent post-publish rollbacks.

Goal: Create a deterministic, SLA-driven binding workflow that: 1) generates an 'epochal' performance profile registry per model-version (sequence-length buckets, batch shapes, KV-cache hit rates); 2) binds kernels to models by explicit SLA constraints (p50/p95 latency, tail latency budget) rather than single-number benchmarks; and 3) publishes profiles to the model manifest with a safe canary + automatic fallback plan.

Scope and non-goals: Scope covers the onboarding pipeline (compile stage -> profiler runs -> profile ingest -> manifest pin). Includes tooling for test-run orchestration and publishing to the profile registry. Does NOT include changes to low-level kernel implementations or new kernel engineering.

Acceptance criteria: 
- A reproducible profiling harness can run targeted workload buckets and produce standardized JSON profiles (token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, memory footprint) for MHA, GQA, and MoE variants.
- A registry format (epochal profiles) is defined and implemented in the manifest store; every published model-version can point to 1..N epochal profiles.
- Kernel binding evaluator picks candidate kernels and scores them against SLA constraints; binding decisions are stored in the manifest and visible in the console.
- Canary rollout process: canary binds applied to 1% traffic for 24h with automated error/latency rollback.
- Metric guards (in console and alerts) trigger automatic fallback to previous pin if SLOs are breached.

Design notes / approach: 
1) Profiling harness: extend existing compiler-smoke tests to run shaped workloads (seq_len: [64,128,512,2048], batch: [1,4,16], kv_cache: [cold,hot]) and emit a normalized profile. Each run records environment fingerprint (arch, GPU type, driver) and a deterministic run-id.
2) Epochal registry: profiles are versioned by date and model-version. 'Epochal' means profiles are expected to be valid for a window (e.g., 90 days) and new profiles create a new epoch. Registry stores meta: workload buckets, measured metrics, candidate kernel IDs, and notes about observed regressions.
3) SLA-driven scoring: define a scoring function that maps profile metrics to an SLA pass/fail and then ranks candidates. For example, p95 <= target_latency -> score +10; memory footprint > GPU_avail -> score -100. This yields a top candidate and safe fallback candidate.
4) Manifest publishing: manifest entries include profile epoch id, bound kernel id, scoring reason, and rollout policy. Console shows the active binding and epoch history.
5) Canary & rollback: orchestrate canary via routing policy; monitor token-level latency, error-rate, and tail latency histograms. If breach detected, revert binding and open a postmortem ticket.

Testing & validation: 
- Unit tests for profile serializer and scoring function.
- Integration: small cluster canary tests with synthetic workloads; record latency histograms and compare against profile predictions.
- Long-tail validation: run a stress job emulating burst traffic for MoE sharded experts to validate fallback behavior.

Observability and telemetry: profiles and binding decisions must emit telemetry: profile_id, kernel_id, score, rollout_state. Add traces for compile->profile->publish path. Use existing dashboards as templates and add 'binding health' chart (active bindings with violation counts).

Security and compliance: profiles may contain model identifiers and traces; ensure publishing respects data retention and access controls. No customer data should be captured by the profiling harness during standard runs.

Docs & rollout: Add an onboarding checklist doc (link placeholder) for SREs and Onboard engineers. Document the score parameters and how to tune SLA thresholds per customer tier.

Open questions: 
- What is the canonical SLA granularity for multi-tenant hosted API vs Dedicated? (expect different thresholds)
- Should epoch length be 90 days or tied to model-version promotions?
- Can we reuse existing compile artifact signatures as kernel IDs or introduce a separate kernel registry?

Deliverables: 
- profiling harness + runner in repo/runtime/profiler (PR link placeholder)
- epochal profile registry schema and manifest extension (PR link placeholder)
- scoring service + tests (PR link placeholder)
- console UI hooks for binding visibility (design/UX PR placeholder)
